title: Find where your harvest is lost, and measure it

say: Find where your harvest is lost, and measure it.
This is the video for Module 1 of Post-Harvest Management and Food Preservation.

Growing food takes months of work, seed and rain. Yet FAO, the United Nations food agency, estimates that about 13 percent of food produced worldwide is lost after harvest, before it reaches the shops.

say: Food lost on farms, in stores, on lorries and in markets is called food loss. Food thrown away by shops and homes is food waste. We focus on loss, because that is the part you can control.

say: Loss is not only weight. Beans full of weevil holes may weigh almost the same, but the buyer pays less. And mould can make food unsafe.

say: Every crop moves through a chain. At harvest and field drying, late picking splits pods, and rain, birds and goats take their share.

panel.heading: Every crop passes through these stages

say: Beating pods on bare ground scatters and breaks grain. In storage, weevils, mould and rats do the damage.

panel.heading: Every crop passes through these stages

say: On the road, overloaded sacks crush produce, and in the market it wilts before it sells. So you check each stage instead of guessing.

panel.heading: Every crop passes through these stages

say: For example, Hauwa farms cowpea near Kano. Last season she harvested about 1,000 kg. She sat with her daughter and estimated the loss at each stage.

panel.heading: Hauwa traces her cowpea losses
items: Harvest and field drying: 40 kg lost
Storage in woven sacks: 150 kg lost
Total 230 kg out of 1,000 kg: 23 percent

say: Pods picked late split open, about 40 kg. Threshing on bare ground, about 30 kg.

panel.heading: Hauwa traces her cowpea losses
items: Harvest and field drying: 40 kg lost
Storage in woven sacks: 150 kg lost
Total 230 kg out of 1,000 kg: 23 percent

say: Six months in ordinary woven sacks, and weevils spoiled about 150 kg. Torn sacks on the way to market spilled about 10 kg.

panel.heading: Hauwa traces her cowpea losses
items: Harvest and field drying: 40 kg lost
Storage in woven sacks: 150 kg lost
Total 230 kg out of 1,000 kg: 23 percent

say: Add them up: 230 kg. Divide by 1,000, and that is 23 percent of her harvest. At about 1,500 naira per kg, that is roughly 345,000 naira.

panel.heading: Hauwa traces her cowpea losses
items: Harvest and field drying: 40 kg lost
Storage in woven sacks: 150 kg lost
Total 230 kg out of 1,000 kg: 23 percent

say: Storage alone was about 65 percent of her loss. So she fixes storage first. Do not try to fix everything at once and run out of money and energy.

panel.rule: Fix the biggest loss point first.

say: Harvested food is still alive and breathing. Durable produce, like maize, cowpea and groundnuts, is low in water once dried. Protect it by drying and sealed storage.
Perishable produce, like tomatoes, ugu, fish and yam, is high in water. It is protected by gentle handling, cooling and fast sale.
Almost every loss comes from five causes. Moisture lets mould grow. Breathing uses up the produce's own sugars and water.

panel.heading: Five causes that feed each other
items: Breathing: produce shrivels and loses taste
Damage: cuts and bruises let rot in

say: Bruises let rot in. Pests eat from the inside. And heat speeds up all of it. They feed each other, so a small damp patch can spoil a bag within weeks.

panel.heading: Five causes that feed each other
items: Breathing: produce shrivels and loses taste
Damage: cuts and bruises let rot in

say: Here is the safety rule. Some moulds make aflatoxins, which WHO links to liver damage and liver cancer. Grain or nuts that look mouldy, discoloured or shrivelled must be discarded, not eaten, sold or fed to children.

panel.heading: Five causes that feed each other
items: Breathing: produce shrivels and loses taste
Damage: cuts and bruises let rot in
panel.rule: Mouldy, discoloured or shrivelled grain: throw it away.

say: Before you change anything, you need a baseline, a measured starting point. Without it, you cannot prove a new method worked.
Take a fair sample from the top, middle and bottom of the bag, mix, and keep one quarter.

cards.d: Take from top, middle and bottom of each bag. Mix on a cloth, divide in four, keep one part.
Sort damaged and undamaged grains, count and weigh both, then use the formula for weight lost.
For each trip, note what you started with, sold at full price, sold at discount, threw away.

say: For grain, use the count-and-weigh method with a kitchen scale.
When Hauwa checked her store after five months, 30 percent of her beans were holed, and the weight loss was 7.5 percent. Record both. Holes cut the price, weight loss cuts the stock.

say: For fresh produce, keep a record for at least three trips. One ugu seller threw away 15 bundles out of 120. That is 12.5 percent, her baseline.

say: Now walk your store and tick each line honestly.
Dry roof. Bags on pallets, which can be planks on bricks. A gap from the walls. No old grain or dust, where insects wait for the new harvest. Rat holes blocked. Dryness tested.
Every no is a likely cause of loss you can fix cheaply.

panel.heading: Store readiness check
items: Bags on pallets, off the floor

say: To remember. Loss is weight, quality, and sometimes safety. Add up losses stage by stage, and fix the biggest one first.
Never eat, sell or feed mouldy grain or nuts. And measure a baseline before you change anything.
